sources: University of Reading news, 'Secret lives of skin mites in our faces' (2022, on Smith et al., Molecular Biology and Evolution, doi:10.1093/molbev/msac125): carried by almost every human; about 0.3 mm long; live in hair follicles on the face, including the eyelashes; eat the sebum in the pores; active at night, moving between follicles looking to mate; passed from mother to baby during or after birth; legs powered by three single-cell muscles; cannot make melatonin and use the melatonin human skin secretes at dusk; lost the gene that makes animals wake in daylight; the study confirmed they do have anuses; numbers peak in adults as pores grow bigger; https://www.reading.ac.uk/news/2022/Research-News/Secret-lives-of-skin-mites-in-our-faces

Thoms et al. (2014), 'Ubiquity of Demodex mites in humans', PLOS ONE 9(8): e106265: Demodex DNA detected in 100% of adults over 18 sampled (n = 19); https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0106265

DermNet (New Zealand Dermatological Society), Demodex: semi-transparent elongated body about 0.3-0.4 mm, eight short legs on the front body segment, invisible to the naked eye; most people carry them without symptoms; https://dermnetnz.org/topics/demodex

title: Tiny Mites Live in Your Face Right Now

beats.say: Tiny mites are living in your face right now.
Demodex. They live in your pores, even your eyelashes.
They eat the oil your skin makes.
At night, they crawl out of your pores,
and walk across your face to find a mate.
One study found their DNA on every adult it tested.
You likely got yours from your mom, at birth.
Subscribe. Part four is in your books.
